site: The Iron Bridge over the River Severn, Ironbridge Gorge near Coalbrookdale, Shropshire. Chapter 11, `ch11_industrial`, site slug `iron_bridge`, painter id `iron-bridge`, asset id `map-monument-ch11-industrial`. Work began November 1777. The masonry abutments went up in 1777–78, the ribs were raised in summer 1779 and first spanned the river on 2 July 1779. The bridge opened on 1 January 1781. It was scheduled as an Ancient Monument in 1934 (18 January, per current Wikipedia as quoted in search results) and closed to vehicles with effect from 18 June 1934. Pedestrian tolls ended in 1950, when ownership passed to Shropshire County Council. It is Grade I listed and part of the Ironbridge Gorge World Heritage Site (1986). English Heritage's £3.6 million conservation of 2017–18 returned it to the very dark red-brown found by paint analysis, and the bridge reopened fully at the end of 2018.
view:
The downstream (east) face, seen from the riverside a short way downstream, with the eye low near the water, looking upstream (west). Downstream really is east here: Buildwas is upstream of Ironbridge and Coalport downstream. The 2019 Commons photograph of the red-brown paint is captioned 'east side'.

Squared up almost to an elevation, turned only enough that the four rib frames behind the face rib show as receding arcs inside the opening.

Frame (92 × 70, painted 368 × 280, edge to edge):
- **Centre:** the main arch, about 60–65% of the plate width, with its crown and humped deck in the upper third.
- **Left (south):** the stone pier at the south foot of the span, then the first of the two small cast-iron land arches, cut by the frame edge or riverside trees. The tollhouse shows only as a pitched dark grey roof, a chimney and a strip of upper wall behind the deck's south end. Historic England's list entry places it at the south end, 'built against its west side', with its upper storey at bridge level, so from this downstream side the bridge end hides all but its top. The July 2020 photograph taken from this side, re-examined this session, shows exactly that: roof and chimney above the deck behind the left-hand stone pier.
- **Right (north):** solid buff-grey masonry of the north abutment running into the bank. Any town houses go up the hillside above right, never on the left.
- **Behind:** steep deciduous woods on both gorge sides rising above deck level, with a band of sky only at the top.
- **Foreground:** the Severn across the full width, with the arch's reflection.

**Why this view.** It is the one standpoint that gets the whole single span, the river it was built to clear for masted boats, and the wooded gorge into one small picture. The arch and its reflection read as a ring even at 92 px. The asymmetric ends (land arches and tollhouse left, masonry right) tell a knowing viewer which way they are facing. It is also the view the first artists took: William Williams painted it from mid-river in 1780. A brochure moves the photographer onto the bank and squares the face up.

**Cropped out:**
- the second land arch and the south approach
- St Luke's church, which stands due north of the bridge up the hill, off the right edge
- the town's riverfront, behind the viewer's right shoulder
- any other bridge downstream

elements.fact: A single cast-iron arch of 100 ft 6 in (30.63 m) with no pier in the river, near-semicircular. Ressler calls the arch rings 'semicircular'. Petroski-derived text says the reflection 'completes the semicircular structure to form a wide-open eye'. The code and the README already say semicircular. A 2026 search summary of the EBSCO Research Starter 'Construction of the First Iron Bridge' also gives a 'single-span semicircular arch' of about 100 ft.

Five parallel cast-iron rib frames (Wikipedia 2017 citing engineering-timelines; Ressler; EBSCO Research Starter: 'five arch ribs, each cast in two halves'). Each main rib was cast in two halves, about 70 ft long and about 5¼–5½ tons each, bolted together at the crown (EB 9th ed.: 'Each of the ribs consisted of two pieces'). From the viewpoint only the face rib is seen whole; the other four recede under the arch.

Three concentric arcs. The innermost runs from support to support and meets the deck at mid-span. The two outer ones rise from the supports and end where they meet the deck, short of the crown (Ressler). EB 7th ed. (Thomas Young) calls them 'the exterior concentric arches which assist in supporting the roadway'. The 2009 photograph shows the three arcs meeting the deck at three different points.
Short members between the three concentric arcs hold them in line, 'amazingly similar to the voussoir joints' of a stone arch, and are dovetailed to the rings (Ressler). The count was not verified.

Vertical iron posts at each end of the span carry the deck load straight down to the foundations, braced by intersecting horizontal members with mortise-and-tenon joints (Ressler). Photographs show a pair of uprights at the north end next to the masonry.

Decorative rings and ogees between the structural ribs; the same elements appear in a gazebo Pritchard rebuilt (Wikipedia 2017, citing Smith 1979 and the Historic England list entry 1219113). Photographs (2009 grey, 2020 red-brown) show one full ring near each end of the face, beside the end uprights, with reverse-curve (ogee) members forming a pointed loop between the uprights. None of this is at the crown.

Carried over the crown with a slight upward peak, because the semicircular arch stands a little higher than the banks (Ressler). The photographs show it rising gently to mid-span. The road surface has been lightened twice: macadam in 1972–75, steel plates with a light top surface in 1999–2002. Neither is visible from below.

A cast-iron parapet of close-set thin vertical bars between taller posts, painted the same red-brown (photos from 2020). A 30 ft length of parapet fell into the river on 24 August 1902, so parts are renewals.

A very dark red-brown, a mahogany shade. English Heritage's own press texts (quoted in search results this session): 'Detailed analysis of those samples revealed that the world's first iron bridge was originally painted in a very dark red-brown lead-based oil paint'. The paint consultant Crick-Smith's microscopic analysis concluded 'the earliest paint was a lead oil-paint, dark red-brown in colour'. Six painters applied 2,400 litres to return it to that colour during the £3.6 million 2017–18 conservation; the bridge was fully reopened at the end of 2018. English Heritage says the result matches William Williams's 1780 painting. Before that it was 'black or slate grey' for decades, grey-blue by 2017 (grey in the 2009 photograph). In the 20th century it was not painted at all until 1980 (Wikipedia 2017).

Masonry, built 1777–78. The stone was renewed in 1972–75, when fill was taken out of the south abutment and its arch was reinforced. In the photographs it reads as buff-grey ashlar with pale lichen patches. The north abutment rises to deck level with a tall stone pier at the corner.

Two supplementary cast-iron arches on the south (Broseley) bank carry a towpath and act as flood arches. Cracks appeared in the original stone land arch there in December 1784. The stone arches were replaced with timber in repairs begun in 1800 (Smiles: 'two small land arches were, in the year 1800, substituted for the stone approach on the Broseley side'). The timber gave way to the present cast iron in December 1820 (Wikipedia 2017, citing Cossons & Trinder p. 50).

Solid masonry into the town bank. A stone arch carries a small path through it on the north (town) bank (Wikipedia 2017). A retaining wall of 35 yards was built in July 1783 to stop the north bank sliding.

Historic England list entry 1279735 (Grade II, 'Former Toll House of the Iron Bridge', quoted in search results): at the south end of the bridge and 'built against its west side'; red brick; three storeys with the upper storey at bridge level; two windows (now bricked up) with segmental heads; plain eaves; a tile roof, not slate; dated early 19th century. Tolls were charged from the opening on 1 January 1781, but this building is not of 1781: a local-history source's claim that the tollhouse was 'open for business' from that date refers to the toll, not this building. The January 2020 photograph looks north over the bridge to the town with the tollhouse on its left, its roof reading dark grey and a chimney stack on the gable. It became redundant when tolls ended in 1950, was opened as an information centre by the Ironbridge Gorge Museum Trust (1972, per the local source) and is now run as 'Iron Bridge and Tollhouse'.

Flows west to east here, from Buildwas upstream to Coalport downstream. Its banks are steep and prone to landslides, with over 20 recorded in the British Geological Survey database for the area. In the photographs the water is dark olive-green, not blue.
Steep wooded sides above deck level on both banks. The trees are deciduous: bare and just leafing in an April 2009 photograph, in full leaf in July 2020.
The town grew up at the north end of the bridge and took its name from it. Looking north along the roadway, the Tontine Hotel and St Luke's church stand directly ahead up the hill.

The outer ribs carry the raised words 'This Bridge was cast at Coalbrook-Dale and erected in the year MDCCLXXIX' (Commons description of Ironbridge2.jpg). The words run along the outer rib near the crown, visible in the July 2020 photograph.

mustBeRight: One single arch spans the river; no pier stands in the water.
The arch is a near-semicircle: round-topped, about twice as wide as it is high, not pointed and not flattened.
On the face rib, three concentric arcs: the innermost runs foot to foot and meets the deck at mid-span; the two outer arcs start at the feet and stop where they meet the deck, short of the crown.
No vertical struts stand between the arch and the deck across the middle of the span.
Vertical iron uprights stand at each end of the span, from the arch's foot up to the deck.
One full ring (an open circle, not a solid disc) sits under the deck near each end, beside the uprights: two rings on the visible face, mirror images, none at the crown.
Reverse-curve (ogee) members sit in the spandrel next to each ring and the uprights.
The deck passes over the crown and rises gently to mid-span; it is neither flat nor steeply humped.
A see-through railing of close-set thin vertical bars runs along the deck edge.
All the ironwork, railings included, is one very dark red-brown (mahogany): not grey, black, silver, pillar-box red or bright rust-orange.
Under the arch, further ribs recede behind the face rib as parallel arcs; if they can be counted there are exactly five ribs.
The iron springs from buff-grey stone masonry at both ends; no brick in the bridge itself.
The two ends differ: at the left (south) end, beyond a stone pier, at least one small iron land arch continues the bridge; the right (north) end runs straight into solid masonry.
A small house with a pitched dark roof and a chimney (the tollhouse) shows behind the left end of the deck, partly hidden by it; nothing like it at the right end.
Steep slopes of deciduous trees rise above deck level on both sides; sky shows only above them.
The river runs under the arch in the foreground and reflects it.
Any town houses are on the right (north) side only.
No vehicles on the bridge.
No lettering anywhere, including on the ribs.
No second bridge and no cooling towers in view.
deliberatelyWrong: The cast inscription along the outer ribs is left off ('This Bridge was cast at Coalbrook-Dale and erected in the year MDCCLXXIX'). The game carries no text, and at 92 × 70 it would be a smudge that reads as dirt.

The colour is the fresh, even post-2018 dark red-brown. A real mid-century brochure would have shown an unpainted, weathered bridge: it was not painted at all in the 20th century until 1980, and in 1950 it 'had not been cleaned or painted for many years'. Red-brown is chosen because it is both the colour the bridge wore new (English Heritage's paint analysis: 'a very dark red-brown lead-based oil paint') and the colour it wears today, so it is right at either end of the story.
The face is squared up more than any riverbank standpoint allows, as a brochure artist would redraw it, so it reads as an elevation.
The radial links, the cross-bracing between the five ribs and the dovetail and mortise joinery are reduced to a few strokes. The real count was not verified and does not survive at vignette size.
The railing is simplified to a regular comb of bars between plain posts; the real posts carry cast decoration.
The second south land arch, the south approach and St Luke's church are cropped out by the frame or trees.
The small stone path arch through the north abutment is hidden behind riverside growth, not drawn. Its exact form was not verified here.
The toll board at the tollhouse (a table of tolls, all text) is not shown.
The cracks, some left untouched and some pinned with wrought-iron straps, are not shown. They are invisible at this size and belong to the level's flaw beat, not the map.
The sky is the set's shared brochure sky, cleaner and bluer than the Severn Gorge usually gets.

palette.name: Iron paint, sunlit face
palette.material: Cast iron in the 2018 paint, face of the ribs and deck fascia in full sun. English Heritage calls the colour 'very dark red-brown', a mahogany shade, so the sunlit value stays inside the measured midday range rather than the warmer dawn reading: midday January railings measure about #845038 to #926349; the deck fascia at dawn measures #a3653c, which is the warm light, not the paint.

palette.name: Iron paint, base
palette.material: The same paint as a local colour, for the painter's brush to light and shade. Darkened from the earlier #7f4230 to match English Heritage's 'very dark red-brown'.

palette.name: Abutment stone, shade

palette.name: Tollhouse roof
palette.material: The tile roof (Historic England: 'tile roof', not slate) and chimney caps. The tiles read a weathered dark grey in the January and July 2020 photographs, so the hex stays a dark warm grey; the exact tile colour was not measured in sun.

palette.name: River Severn
palette.material: The Severn's water, olive-green and reflecting the wooded gorge. In shade it measures about #212718 and in open water #3e4327 in the 2009 photograph. Use this instead of the set's shared water (#4f8fb9), which is too blue for this river.

palette.name: River, lit ripples and reflected sky
palette.material: Broken highlights on the river where it reflects the sky between the arch's reflection and the banks.

palette.name: Riverbank earth
palette.material: Muddy bank and towpath at the water's edge below the abutments.

lighting:
Keep the set's sun, upper right. For a view facing west this is a north-easterly sun low over the viewer's right shoulder. That is true on a summer morning here, not a brochure lie: at 52.63°N near midsummer the sun stays north of due east until about 07:17 local solar time, roughly 08:30 BST, at up to about 30° altitude. The photograph taken at 05:58 BST on 31 July 2020 from this side shows the downstream face lit warmly from the right.

What is lit and what is in shade:
- **Lit:** the face rib, its rings and ogees, the deck fascia, the railing and the viewer-facing masonry of both abutments.
- **Cool shade:** the underside of the arch, the four ribs receding behind the face rib, the left (shadow) sides of the uprights and piers, and the tollhouse's near wall.
- **Woods:** the slopes behind stay darker than the bridge, so the red-brown frame reads against them. Use the set's foliage for the sunlit canopy and foliageDark for the shaded slopes.
- **Reflection:** darker and slightly broken, closing the arch into a near-ring.
- **Shadows:** the deck may cast a thin shadow onto the upper spandrel.

Use the set's shared sky, sun, shadow and ink.
pitfalls: Painting it grey, silver or black. Most photographs from before 2018 show the grey paint of c. 1980–2017 (grey in 2009; 'black or slate grey' for decades, grey-blue by 2017), and many assume cast iron is black. Most early prints are monochrome engravings too: of at least 47 known images before 1845, all but four are grey-black engravings.
Painting it bright orange rust or pillar-box red. It is a very dark red-brown, a mahogany shade. Dawn photographs make it look orange; that is the light.
Giving the tollhouse a slate roof or dating it to 1781. The list entry has a tile roof and an early-19th-century date.
Copying the current code silhouette: vertical struts from the arch to the deck across the haunches. The real spandrel is filled by two more concentric ribs that die into the deck, plus radial links.
Putting the rings at the crown or mid-haunch, painting them as solid discs, or leaving out the ogees. The rings sit near the ends beside the uprights.
A flat deck and flat railing. The deck peaks gently over the crown.
Making the ends symmetrical, putting the iron land arches at the north end, or leaving them out altogether.
Putting the tollhouse at the town (north) end, or in front of the bridge on the downstream side. It is at the south end, on the upstream side of the approach.
Putting the town on the tollhouse side. The town is on the north bank, the right side from downstream.
Letting the arch spring from bare slopes or float. Both ends stand on masonry, and the deck ends land on stone.
A single flat frame with no depth. The bridge is five ribs wide.
Rivets, lattice girders or wrought-iron trusswork. It is cast iron joined like carpentry: dovetails, mortise and tenon, and bolts at the crown.
A pointed, elliptical or flattened arch.
Blue, clear water. The Severn in the gorge is olive-green and brown.
Adding traffic. No vehicle has crossed since 18 June 1934.

Adding any downstream bridge: the Jackfield Free Bridge (a reinforced-concrete two-arch bridge of 1909, replaced by the present Jackfield Bridge, reopened 18 October 1994) or the Coalport bridge. Also leave out the Ironbridge power-station cooling towers, which appear in photographs until their demolition on 6 December 2019.
Conifer forest. The gorge woods are deciduous broadleaf.
Painting the cast inscription or the toll board as lettering.
gate6: clear. Engineering, a scheduled monument and a working footbridge. No worship, no graves, no atrocity. The Coalport ferry drowning of 1799 happened downstream at Coalport, not here, and nothing of it is in frame. The no-text rule, not gate 6, keeps the cast inscription and the toll board out.
contested: Who designed it. The rings and ogees match a gazebo Pritchard rebuilt, which suggests the final design was his (Wikipedia 2017, citing Smith 1979). Smiles (1863) says Pritchard's plan used iron only at the crown and was set aside for a design by Darby's pattern-maker Thomas Gregory. Pevsner says the executed design is 'probably Abraham Darby's'. Keep open.

The reading of Williams's 1780 painting. Before 2018 it was read as rust on unpainted iron (Wikipedia caption, January 2017: 'rust-red in colour, suggesting that it was unpainted'). English Heritage's 2018 paint analysis (Crick-Smith, microscopic sampling) found the earliest coat was a dark red-brown lead oil paint and says the painting shows that paint, so the rust reading is superseded for the bridge's colour. What remains open is only how literally Williams recorded it; the other early colour images disagree in shade (Robertson 1788 'dark red', Varley c. 1802 'reddy-brown', Westwood 1835 'pinkish'). Simple English Wikipedia dates the painting 1777, which is wrong: it is 1780.

The number of parts. Older accounts (Wikipedia 2007) give 'more than 800 castings of 12 basic types'; later ones (Wikipedia 2017, citing engineering-timelines) give 'almost 1,700 individual components'.
The weight. 378½ tons (EB 7th ed.; Wikipedia's '378 long tons 10 cwt'), '379 tons' (Wikipedia 2007) and 'nearly 400 tons' (popular accounts). The figures are close.

The height. 'Rising to 60 feet above the river' (Wikipedia 2007; a 2026 secondary summary says 60 ft above high water, to the deck, not the arch's rise) against 'the main arch spans 100 feet and it's 40 feet high' (Ressler), though Ressler also calls the arch rings semicircular. The painting follows the near-semicircular shape that all sources and photographs agree on, not a figure.
The opening date. 1 January 1781 (Cossons & Trinder via Wikipedia; local sources). Smiles (1863) says 'opened for traffic in 1779', running it together with the 1779 erection.

The land-arch dates. Smiles puts 'two small land arches' on the Broseley side in 1800. Wikipedia 2007 has the south stone abutment demolished by 1802 and replaced by temporary timber arches. Wikipedia 2017 (Cossons & Trinder) has timber from repairs begun in 1800 and cast iron from December 1820.

Where tolls were taken before the present tollhouse. Tolls were charged from 1 January 1781, but the standing tollhouse is dated early 19th century by its list entry (1279735). Whether an earlier toll building stood there was not established.

Text: the English Heritage project cost £3.6 million and 'returned the bridge to its original red-brown colour (which took 2400 litres of paint)'; the tollhouse was open for business from 1 January 1781 and the Ironbridge Gorge Museum Trust opened it as a Tourist Information Centre in 1972; the cooling towers were demolished on 6 December 2019. Its photographs (the photographer's copyright, for reference only, never for the repository) were examined and colour-sampled: 1shropshire/assets/images/history/2009-04-19_17-41-55_00006342.jpg (grey paint, north end, rings and ogees, south pier and land arch), 2020-07-31_05_58_17_DSC_7646.jpg (red-brown, from the downstream north bank, tollhouse behind the south end, the inscription on the outer rib, lit from the right at 05:58 BST), and 2020-01-12_12_28_07_DSC_6193.jpg (tollhouse on the west of the south approach, red-brown railings, the town and St Luke's to the north). All three were downloaded again from raw.githubusercontent.com and viewed directly in the verification pass of 2026-09-23: the July 2020 view confirms the stone pier and iron land arch at the left end, solid masonry at the right, the deck and railing rising to mid-span, and the tollhouse's dark roof and chimney above the deck at the left; the January 2020 view confirms the tollhouse on the left looking north, its dark roof and gable chimney, and St Luke's tower ahead.

repoCorrections: src/map/monuments.ts, 'iron-bridge': the four vertical struts from the arch to the deck at x = 32, 41, 59, 68 do not exist on the bridge.
